posts.title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta
posts.summary: Some AI data centers are retrofitting retired jet engines to burn natural gas because grid connections and new turbines are taking years to come online. The converted units can be deployed in as little as 24 months, a stark contrast to the seven‑year timeline for a 100‑MW grid hookup in Northern Virginia. Companies such as xAI, OpenAI, and the Denver‑based Crusoe have already installed or ordered dozens of these engines, while others have abandoned larger turbine deals in favor of the quicker solution. Although the jet‑engine turbines are less efficient and more polluting than purpose‑built gas plants, they offer a short‑term fix that may become less attractive as efficiency and environmental concerns rise.
key_points: Retired jet engines are being converted to natural‑gas turbines to power AI data centers quickly.
Deployment can be achieved in about 24 months, compared to 7 years for conventional grid connections.
Major players like xAI, OpenAI, and Crusoe are already using or ordering these units.
The technology is less efficient and more polluting, making it a temporary solution.

posts.title: Netflix's new AI Discover tab helps you find something to watch based on your mood | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Netflix has launched an AI Discover tab that lets users find shows based on their current mood, offering curated themes such as "scare me" and "quick watches". The feature uses a new AI layer that learns from real‑time user input and lets viewers tune recommendations by adding or excluding titles. Netflix calls the tab a "test kitchen" where it experiments with discovery options and collects feedback before integrating them into the main experience. The rollout began in the U.S. for English‑TV users and will expand to other markets in the coming weeks.
key_points: Netflix introduces an AI Discover tab for mood‑based recommendations
Curated themes and a Tune Your Recommendations button let users refine suggestions
The tab serves as a test kitchen for new discovery features and gathers user feedback
Initial rollout is in the U.S. for English‑TV users with plans for broader expansion

posts.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ram Iyer
posts.summary: CrowdStrike announced acquisitions of Fiddler AI and Dreadnode for roughly $400 million and $95 million respectively, expanding its Falcon platform to monitor and test AI agents and models. The deals come as enterprises deploy AI agents at scale, creating new security gaps that traditional tools struggle to cover. Fiddler AI will become Falcon Observe, providing observability of agent behavior, while Dreadnode will feed automated security testing into Falcon Guardian. These moves position CrowdStrike to capture a growing market for AI‑centric security solutions.
key_points: CrowdStrike is paying about $400 million for Fiddler AI and $95 million for Dreadnode to broaden its AI security offerings
Fiddler AI will be integrated as Falcon Observe to monitor AI agent behavior, while Dreadnode will enhance Falcon Guardian with automated testing
The acquisitions address the security challenges posed by widespread AI agent deployment across enterprises
The moves aim to capture a rapidly expanding market for AI‑centric security solutions

posts.title: Exclusive: Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Also, a micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly abandoned an electric two‑wheeler pilot in Kenya after receiving a Shell Foundation grant, choosing instead to concentrate on its consumer e‑bike TM‑B and autonomous vehicle work. The Kenya project, aimed at creating a locally integrated electric motorcycle for African riders, was halted after early‑stage work and a shift in priorities toward DoorDash‑partnered small autonomous vehicles. Supply‑chain disruptions delayed the launch of Also’s flagship TM‑B, causing customer frustration and communication gaps, but the company has begun shipping units in early October and is improving its outreach. The move underscores Also’s focus on scalable, cost‑optimized vehicles and its broader ambitions to sell commercial cargo bikes to firms like Amazon.
key_points: Also withdrew from a Shell Foundation‑funded Kenya electric‑motorcycle pilot to focus on its e‑bike TM‑B and autonomous vehicle roadmap.
Supply‑chain challenges delayed the TM‑B launch, leading to customer frustration and a communication overhaul.
The company is partnering with DoorDash on small autonomous vehicles and plans commercial cargo bikes for Amazon.
The Kenya project aimed to test modular batteries and distributed charging for African riders but was abandoned after early‑stage work.

posts.title: Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Google announced it will disable its AI tools for K‑12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on, a move that also removes Google Search from schools that opt out because AI features are now embedded in the search engine. The change follows consultations with educators, researchers and policymakers and reflects Google’s intent to give school leaders control over AI use while maintaining its dominant suite of classroom apps. Schools that want to keep access to Search will have to accept its AI features, creating a trade‑off between search functionality and AI restrictions. Google also unveiled Guided Learning, an AI tutor designed to help students build deeper understanding rather than just provide answers.
key_points: Google will disable AI tools for K‑12 unless administrators enable them
Disabling AI also disables Google Search for those schools
Schools face a trade‑off between search access and AI restrictions
Google launched Guided Learning, an AI tutor for deeper learning

posts.title: Ted Schlein's Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Ballistic Ventures, a San Francisco‑based cybersecurity VC founded in 2021 by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein, has filed to raise $490 million across two new vehicles: a $360 million third flagship fund and a $130 million separate Fund B. The move comes amid a surge in AI‑driven cyber threats, which has pushed U.S. cybersecurity startups to raise $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest total since 2022, and made AI‑enabled companies account for 72% of deals through May. Ballistic’s founding team—comprising Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton—has backed notable firms such as Talon Cyber Security, Pangea, and others, positioning the firm to capitalize on the growing intersection of AI and cybersecurity.
key_points: Ballistic Ventures is raising $490M across a $360M flagship fund and a $130M Fund B to support AI‑driven cybersecurity startups
AI‑enabled cyber threats have driven 72% of U.S. cybersecurity deals through May, contributing to a record $11.5B raised in 2025
The firm’s founders include Ted Schlein, Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton, and it has backed companies like Talon Cyber Security and Pangea
Ballistic’s fundraising reflects the broader trend of venture capital focusing on cybersecurity amid rising AI‑powered attack capabilities

posts.title: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Fal, a San Francisco-based AI inference startup, has doubled its valuation to $16 billion after closing a $1.3 billion Series F round led by Bessemer Venture Partners and joined by Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The company announced that the combined Series E and Series F rounds raised $1.65 billion, with Sequoia having led the earlier round. Fal’s annualized revenue exceeded $800 million earlier this year, underscoring the rapid growth of demand for inference services that run pre‑trained AI models. The valuation jump highlights the high expectations for inference providers, even as many face thin margins due to costly compute resources.
key_points: Fal’s valuation doubled to $16 billion after a $1.3 billion Series F round led by Bessemer Venture Partners.
The combined Series E and Series F rounds raised $1.65 billion, with Nvidia and Bessemer as key investors.
Fal’s annualized revenue surpassed $800 million, reflecting the surge in demand for AI inference services.

posts.title: Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Reddit is testing ad placements in its search results pages as it faces a decline in search traffic and a weaker-than‑expected revenue outlook. The company announced the trial on Tuesday, offering contextual ads that match users’ search queries, such as espresso‑related products for a search on "espresso station." The move comes after the platform beat earnings estimates but issued fourth‑quarter guidance below Wall Street expectations, citing reduced traffic from Google’s AI‑powered search. Reddit also plans a gradual shift to a logged‑in experience to protect against AI scraping and to provide advertisers with richer user data, potentially boosting ad revenue.
key_points: Reddit is launching contextual search‑result ads to offset declining search traffic and strengthen monetization.
Q3 revenue beat expectations but fourth‑quarter guidance fell short, largely due to AI‑driven traffic loss from Google.
The company is moving toward a logged‑in user model to enhance ad targeting and guard against AI scraping.
The new ad test and login shift aim to increase revenue from existing users amid flat or falling daily active user numbers.

posts.title: Anthropic is still grappling with the economics of compute | TechCrunch
posts.author: Russell Brandom
posts.summary: Anthropic disclosed that its compute costs now consume 58% of revenue, up from 48% a quarter earlier, even as revenue rose to $17 billion. The company’s operating loss grew because a $10 billion compute bill—half of it under short‑term contracts—outpaced revenue gains. Anthropic is still courting high‑rate neoclouds such as SpaceX, Nscale, Akamai and Volta while working on its own “Anthropic Direct” compute base, but the rapid demand growth keeps costs high. The worsening margins highlight the vulnerability of AI labs to infrastructure pricing as they near IPO and seek investor confidence.
key_points: Compute costs rose to 58% of revenue, up from 48% a quarter earlier
Anthropic’s $10 billion compute bill included $5 billion under short‑term commitments
Revenue grew to $17 billion but operating loss widened
The firm relies on high‑rate neoclouds and is developing its own compute base under Anthropic Direct

posts.title: Hiding inside Palantir's skyrocketing quarter is a foreboding signal | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Palantir reported a record third‑quarter revenue of $2.31 billion, up 96% year‑over‑year and 20% from the prior quarter, beating analysts’ $2.18 billion forecast and marking the first time the company topped $2 billion in a single quarter. The company also posted adjusted earnings per share of 44 cents versus the expected 41 cents, and raised its full‑year revenue guidance to more than $3.559 billion, a 143% growth rate. However, enterprise sales showed signs of slowing, with total contract value falling from $2.13 billion in the previous quarter to $1.46 billion, and CEO Alex Karp warned that many corporate customers are signing short‑term trials that may be cancelled. Despite the upbeat numbers, the mixed signals about enterprise adoption and contract longevity raise questions about Palantir’s long‑term growth trajectory.
key_points: Palantir’s Q3 revenue hit $2.31 billion, the first time it exceeded $2 billion in a quarter and beat consensus expectations
U.S. commercial revenue ($984 million) surpassed U.S. government revenue ($953 million) for the first time, yet total contract value fell from $2.13 billion to $1.46 billion, indicating slowing sales
CEO Alex Karp highlighted that many enterprise customers are engaging in short‑term trials that can be cancelled, signaling a potential churn risk
The company raised its full‑year commercial revenue guidance to over $3.559 billion, projecting at least 143% growth

posts.title: Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Orbital Matter’s Replicator 2 satellite, launched on a SpaceX rideshare, 3D‑printed a half‑meter rigid beam in orbit, marking the first time a free‑flying spacecraft has built a structural element in space. The demonstration shows that in‑orbit manufacturing can create large solar arrays and other components, potentially easing the power and heat‑dissipation challenges of future orbital data centers. The company plans a 2028 mission that will test a larger printer capable of producing a 5 kW solar array, with a goal of 100+ kW arrays by 2030. Orbital Matter is partnering with ESA, Thales Alenia, NASA and Redwire to integrate its printer‑assisted deployment system into commercial satellites.
key_points: First rigid beam (0.5 m) 3D‑printed in orbit by Orbital Matter’s Replicator 2
In‑orbit manufacturing can enable large solar arrays and structures, easing power and heat challenges
Planned 2028 mission aims for a 5 kW solar array, targeting 100+ kW arrays by 2030
Collaborations with ESA, Thales Alenia, NASA and Redwire to integrate the technology into commercial satellites

posts.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Binance confirmed that a North Korean hacking group used a months‑long social engineering campaign to trick a wallet‑team engineer into downloading malicious code, which then allowed the attackers to compromise multiple systems and steal a record $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. The attackers posed as recruiters offering a job, sending a fake coding assignment that contained malware, and later leveraged credentials stolen from a second engineer who had previously downloaded a tampered app. The incident prompted Binance to suspend withdrawals, review its security posture, and bring in external cybersecurity experts. The heist underscores the persistent threat posed by state‑sponsored actors targeting the crypto industry through elaborate social‑engineering tactics.
key_points: North Korean hackers used fake recruiter personas to infect Binance’s systems via a malicious coding assignment
The attack exploited multiple compromised engineer accounts, enabling access to a tool that controls billions of dollars in crypto
Binance has suspended withdrawals, upgraded security measures, and engaged external experts after the theft

posts.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Google has expanded its experimental AI app Dreambeans to India, making it the first market outside the U.S. The launch includes support for 13 local languages, such as Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, and English, and leverages data from Google services like Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube to generate personalized illustrated and animated stories. While the app has seen modest downloads in the U.S., its entry into India aims to tap a large user base that frequently uses Google’s ecosystem, though language mixing and privacy concerns may limit adoption. Google says users can control which services feed the app, delete data, and set content filters to mitigate sensitive or unwanted stories.
key_points: Dreambeans is now available in India with 13 language options, targeting a market that heavily uses Google services.
The app automatically creates personalized visual stories from users’ Google data without prompts, adding animated elements via Veo.
Privacy controls let users choose connected services, delete data, and filter content, but the reliance on personal data raises concerns.
Downloads in the U.S. peaked in September but fell sharply in October, indicating early adoption challenges.

posts.title: Anthropic warns that it's very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Anthropic’s revised S‑1/A filing reveals the company believes it is on the brink of creating a model capable of recursive self‑improvement (RSI), a milestone that could accelerate AI progress dramatically. The lab acknowledges that using AI to build more capable AI poses significant safety risks and has outlined a Responsible Scaling Policy to monitor and mitigate those risks. While no current model has crossed the RSI threshold, Anthropic stresses that human oversight will remain integral to frontier model development. The announcement underscores the dual promise and peril of RSI and signals the need for proactive governance as AI capabilities surge.
key_points: Anthropic says it is close to achieving recursive self‑improvement, a milestone that could accelerate AI progress dramatically.
The company has a Responsible Scaling Policy to monitor and mitigate safety risks associated with rapid AI development.
No current model has yet crossed the RSI threshold, and human oversight will continue to guide frontier model creation.
Rapid progress could outpace safety measures, prompting the need for proactive governance and regulation.

posts.title: New York City's Mamdani criticizes Madison Square Garden owner over surveillance tech | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized Madison Square Garden owner James Dolan for using surveillance and facial‑recognition technology, arguing it violates privacy and should be banned. He praised local legislation introduced by Councilmember Shahana Hanif that would prohibit biometric data collection in public spaces. Wired reports reveal MSG maintains a database that flags visitors, including celebrities, as LGBTQIA and has used facial‑recognition to identify a lawyer who sued the company, leading to a lawsuit against Wired. MSG denies the claims and says it is pursuing legal remedies, while New York City has required businesses to disclose biometric data collection since 2021.
key_points: NYC Mayor Mamdani calls for banning MSG's facial‑recognition surveillance and supports new biometric‑data legislation.
Wired exposed MSG’s database that labels visitors as LGBTQIA and used facial‑recognition to identify a lawyer, prompting a lawsuit.
MSG denies the allegations and is pursuing legal action against Wired.

posts.title: The Founder Summit agenda is only half the reason to be in Boston on Nov. 4 | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 will take place on November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston, bringing founders and investors together for a full day of practical learning, candid conversations, live pitching, roundtables, and networking. The agenda is split into a Build Stage focused on early‑stage decisions like distribution, fundraising, and team building, and an Impact Stage that tackles scaling, product‑market fit, and long‑term growth. Attendees can also participate in focused roundtables on niche challenges, watch founders pitch in real time, and use Braindate to schedule intentional conversations. Ticket offers include a buy‑one‑get‑one‑free deal, up to $100 off individual passes, and up to 30% off group bundles.
key_points: Founder Summit 2026 is scheduled for November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston
The event features Build and Impact stages, roundtables, a live pitch competition, and Braindate networking
Tickets offer a buy‑one‑get‑one‑free deal, up to $100 off, and up to 30% off group bundles
The agenda is designed to provide practical lessons, strategic insights, and networking opportunities for founders

posts.title: Apple restricts dating apps and AI companions to users 18 and up | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple is tightening its App Store policies to restrict dating and AI companion apps to users 18 and older, requiring developers to add new content descriptors and an 18+ rating by November 16. The rule also covers apps that share real‑world locations and aims to protect minors through age assurance technology and enhanced parental controls. Popular AI companion services such as Character.AI, Replika, and xAI could be affected, as they often target younger audiences and offer romantic or sexual content. This move follows Apple’s broader effort to improve child safety across its ecosystem.
key_points: Apple mandates an 18+ rating for all dating and relationship apps on the App Store
Developers must add new content descriptors and comply by November 16
The policy also targets AI companion apps and location‑sharing features
It is part of Apple’s larger initiative to protect minors with age assurance tech and parental controls

posts.title: Tomorrow: Founder Summit takes over Boston and when pass rates increase | TechCrunch
posts.author: TechCrunch Events
posts.summary: TechCrunch’s Founder Summit will take place tomorrow, November 4, at Boston’s SoWa Power Station and is presented by Fidelity Private Shares. The event offers a buy‑one‑get‑one‑free ticket deal and encourages early registration before prices rise at 9 a.m. ET. Attendees can choose between Build and Impact stages that cover fundraising, product‑market fit, scaling, and enterprise relationships, as well as smaller roundtable conversations. The day also features a live pitch competition and a Braindate networking app to facilitate one‑on‑one connections.
key_points: Founder Summit in Boston on Nov 4 at SoWa Power Station presented by Fidelity Private Shares
Buy‑one‑get‑one‑free ticket deal and early price lock before doors open at 9 a.m. ET
Sessions split into Build and Impact stages plus roundtables covering fundraising, product‑market fit, and scaling
Live pitch competition and Braindate app enable networking and one‑on‑one conversations

posts.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe's startup scene | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Yvonne Bajela launched Evertrue Capital, closing an oversubscribed $17M Fund I focused on early‑stage AI and fintech in the UK and Europe. She brings a decade of VC experience from LocalGlobe and Impact X, having backed companies like Wise and Mooves. The fund plans to invest about £350k per deal and target 20 companies over three years, with 80% of LPs UK‑based. Bajela cites the AI boom and a democratized building landscape as reasons for timing, while noting fundraising remains tough even in a supportive UK market.
key_points: Evertrue Capital closed a $17M oversubscribed Fund I focused on early‑stage AI and fintech in the UK and Europe.
The fund will average £350k checks and target 20 companies over three years, backed by 80% UK LPs.
Bajela’s decade of VC experience includes investments in Wise, Marshmallow, and Mooves.
She cites the AI boom and a democratized startup ecosystem as the right timing for launching the fund.

posts.title: Apple Watch's AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple has begun beta testing its new Audio Intelligence suite on the Apple Watch, launching the features in the iOS 27.3 update for developers. The four opt‑in tools include sound and song recognition, Live Rewind—which lets users double‑press the crown to view a 15‑second text snippet of the last conversation—and Siri Recaps, which summarizes conversations into bullet points without recording raw audio. Apple emphasizes privacy by processing audio on the watch’s S11 chip, encrypting data in a secure enclave, and deleting summaries from its Private Cloud Compute immediately after use. The beta will later expand to a public test before the features become available to all users.
key_points: Live Rewind captures a 15‑second snippet of recent speech that can be saved or deleted after 30 seconds
Siri Recaps generates concise, speaker‑agnostic summaries that can be exported to Notes or Journal and are deleted after seven days if not saved
Audio is processed on the watch and iPhone in a secure enclave, with no raw audio stored or sent to Apple
The features are currently in developer beta via iOS 27.3 and will roll out to the public after broader testing

posts.title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Trajectory, a Stanford‑born startup, has raised $45 million in a Series A led by Sequoia and backed by Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures, valuing the 18‑person company at $300 million. The firm offers a continual‑learning platform that lets businesses fine‑tune open‑source AI models with real‑world feedback, enabling lawyers, doctors, and other specialists to improve models without hiring costly research teams. By automating post‑training, Trajectory aims to make specialized AI deployment faster, cheaper, and accessible to nontechnical users. The platform is already used by companies such as Harvey, Rogo, Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia, and it competes with other post‑training startups like Thinking Machines Lab, Applied Compute, and Prime Intellect.
key_points: $45 million Series A at a $300 million valuation led by Sequoia with Nvidia, Bessemer, and Bain Capital Ventures
Trajectory automates continual learning so nontechnical experts can fine‑tune AI models with real‑world feedback
The platform is already adopted by firms in law, finance, and tech, speeding up specialized AI deployment

posts.title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing...something with third-party AI apps | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Apple’s services division, already at record levels, is looking for new revenue streams amid regulatory pressure on the App Store and a slump in mobile gaming.  On its earnings call, CFO Kevan Parekh hinted that AI could drive growth by encouraging customers to upgrade and by opening opportunities with third‑party apps and partnerships.  Investors are speculating that Apple could profit from distributing third‑party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate.  Despite headwinds, Apple projects services growth of 8‑9% for the December quarter.
key_points: Apple may monetize third‑party AI agents via the App Store and take a revenue cut
Regulatory changes and legal challenges have reduced App Store commission revenue in key markets
Apple’s services business remains record‑level, with 8‑9% growth expected in the next quarter
AI is seen as a driver for customer upgrades and new partnership opportunities

posts.title: Germany says lawmakers' iPhones may have been hacked with spyware | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Germany’s federal cybersecurity office warned that members of parliament and other public figures may have been targeted by government‑backed spyware, following Apple’s threat notifications that iPhones could have been compromised. The BSI urged anyone who received a notification to assume their device might be infected, though it did not confirm which officials were affected or which state actors were involved. Apple’s alerts, which flag zero‑click exploits that can silently steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information, have also reached users in 99 countries. The incident underscores the opaque supply chain of mercenary spyware, such as Pegasus from NSO Group, that governments often purchase to surveil political opponents.
key_points: German BSI warned parliament members could have been hit by government‑backed spyware after Apple’s threat alerts.
Apple’s notifications flag zero‑click exploits that can silently steal data, but do not confirm actual compromise or attribution.
The case highlights the use of private spyware vendors like NSO Group’s Pegasus, which many governments purchase.

posts.title: Snap settles lawsuit accusing platform of fueling teen depression and eating disorders | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Snap has settled a lawsuit filed by two teenagers who alleged the platform was designed to be addictive and contributed to their depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. The settlement is part of a broader wave of litigation targeting social media companies for their impact on young users, following similar cases against Meta, TikTok, and YouTube. Snap had already settled other cases scheduled for trial and had expected CEO Evan Spiegel to testify. The company says it has implemented safeguards, safety tutorials, and expert partnerships and remains committed to improving user safety and well‑being.
key_points: Snap reached a settlement with two teen plaintiffs over addiction and mental‑health claims.
The case follows similar lawsuits against Meta, TikTok, and YouTube.
Snap asserts it has introduced safety measures and will continue to strengthen them.
The lawsuit underscores growing legal scrutiny of social media’s influence on youth mental health.

posts.title: Ninja’s first-ever microwave just replaced two of my kitchen appliances at once | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Ninja’s new Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer blends a 1,000‑W microwave with a 1,700‑W air‑fry system in a single unit, using FusionCrisp technology to heat food quickly while giving it a crispy finish. The appliance, priced at $449.99 (discounted to $349.99 on Amazon), features a 5.5‑quart glass dish, a non‑stick crisper plate, and no rotating plate, allowing larger dishes to be cooked at once. While it can replace separate microwave and air‑fryer units and free counter space for those who use both, its 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1‑inch footprint and high price make it less suitable for small kitchens or budget shoppers.
key_points: Ninja’s Crispi combines a 1,000‑W microwave and a 1,700‑W air fryer in one unit using FusionCrisp technology
The appliance costs $449.99 (Amazon $349.99) and measures 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1 inches, offering a large cooking area without a rotating plate
It can replace separate microwave and air‑fryer appliances, freeing counter space for users who regularly use both
Its high price and size make it less ideal for small kitchens or budget‑conscious buyers

posts.title: AI can make tech CEOs’ lives easier. What about everyone else? | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: TechCrunch discusses how AI CEOs such as Marissa Mayer, Sam Altman, and Mark Zuckerberg have made out‑of‑touch remarks about AI’s role in everyday life, sparking criticism. The article questions whether the industry’s focus on optimizing basic human interactions—like dating, parenting, and social needs—really serves the average consumer. A podcast interview with Amanda Silberling explores whether the disconnect stems from marketing missteps, product design choices, or a mismatch between the CEOs’ target audience and the broader public. The discussion highlights growing skepticism about AI’s societal impact and the need for companies to balance innovation with genuine human connection.
key_points: AI CEOs have made remarks that many see as out‑of‑touch, prompting criticism.
The industry’s push to replace basic human interactions with AI may not align with everyday users’ needs.
Amanda Silberling argues the issue is partly marketing and partly product design.
There is increasing societal skepticism about AI’s role in personal and social life.

posts.title: Apple says it's 'hard to predict' when iPhone Duo constraints will improve | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple acknowledged that shipping delays for the iPhone Duo are still ongoing and it is difficult to predict when supply will meet demand, according to COO Sabih Khan on the company’s fiscal fourth‑quarter earnings call. The delays stem from extraordinary demand that caused the device to sell out within hours, coupled with rising memory‑chip costs driven by the AI industry. Apple has reluctantly raised prices on several products and is deepening its titanium partnership with Perryman to support the new foldable phone. Customers who missed pre‑orders are now facing delivery dates that extend into next year, prompting Verizon to offer gift cards as an apology.
key_points: iPhone Duo shipping delays push delivery into next year due to extraordinary demand and supply constraints
Apple has raised prices on several products amid soaring memory‑chip costs
Apple is strengthening its titanium supply partnership with Perryman for the foldable device
Verizon is compensating affected customers with gift cards

posts.title: Apple's inventory surges 154% as memory chip costs climb | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Apple’s inventory rose sharply in fiscal Q4, jumping 31.1% from $11.09 billion in Q3 to $14.54 billion and growing 154.3% year‑over‑year. The surge is largely driven by higher memory chip costs, which the company expects to keep climbing and are a key factor behind its 45‑46% gross‑margin forecast for the December quarter. Apple is increasing memory purchases by $33 billion from June to September, while also raising device prices to offset the cost pressure. Weak iPad sales, down 10% YoY, were attributed to supply constraints amid the broader memory‑cost squeeze.
key_points: Inventory increased 31.1% in Q4 and 154.3% YoY, largely due to memory chip costs
Apple forecasts a 45‑46% gross margin for the December quarter, citing rising memory expenses
The company raised memory purchases by $33 billion from June to September and expects further cost rises
iPad revenue fell 10% YoY to $6.2 billion, reflecting supply constraints and weaker demand

posts.title: Web host Squarespace lays off 19% of its employees | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Squarespace announced a 19% workforce reduction, cutting roughly 300 jobs, as part of a restructuring aimed at streamlining operations and positioning the company for future growth. The move comes amid a broader industry shift toward generative‑AI‑powered website builders, with rivals like Wix and Lovable raising significant capital for similar tools. Squarespace has been investing heavily in AI, launching Blueprint in 2024 and the upcoming Forma platform, and recently returned to private ownership after a $7 billion buyout. The layoffs signal the company’s effort to adapt to changing market dynamics while accelerating its AI strategy.
key_points: Squarespace is cutting about 19% of its workforce, roughly 300 employees, to simplify operations and accelerate growth
The company is investing in AI with products like Blueprint and the upcoming Forma platform
Industry competitors such as Wix and Lovable are raising large sums for AI‑driven website builders
The layoffs reflect a broader shift in web hosting toward generative‑AI tools and a need to stay competitive

posts.title: New York Times and other outlets sue web browser Brave over alleged content scraping | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: The New York Times has filed a federal lawsuit against the privacy‑focused browser Brave, accusing it of scraping the Times’ copyrighted articles and distributing them to AI companies such as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. The suit, which also names the Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel, alleges that Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages with an unidentified crawler, bypassed paywalls, and blocked publishers’ ads while selling its own. The Times calls Brave a "supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content" and seeks an injunction and damages. Brave, founded in 2015 and having raised roughly $250 million, has not yet responded to the complaint.
key_points: The New York Times sued Brave for scraping and distributing its copyrighted content to AI firms.
Multiple other newspapers joined the lawsuit, all filed in Manhattan federal court.
The suit accuses Brave of building a massive web index, bypassing paywalls, and blocking ads.
Brave, founded in 2015 and raised about $250 million, has not yet commented.

posts.title: Y Combinator's Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan revealed that he spends between $100,000 and $200,000 a year on AI tokens to power a suite of agents that handle everything from coding to personal email and notes. He showcased 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub to demonstrate how agents can automate day‑to‑day tasks and even anticipate needs. Tan highlighted YC’s internal agent, Stray Light, which aggregates the entire founder database to streamline operations, and he warned that treating agents like static software limits their human‑like flexibility. He concluded that personal AI agents could become mainstream once costs drop, but cautioned against relying on free agents controlled by large tech firms that may impose algorithmic constraints.
key_points: Tan spends $100k–$200k annually on AI tokens to run a network of agents that manage both work and personal data.
He shares 23 Claude Code skills on GitHub to illustrate how agents can automate tasks and anticipate needs.
YC uses an internal agent, Stray Light, that compiles all founder data to improve operations.
He believes personal AI agents will become mainstream only if prices fall and users retain control over their own models.

posts.title: Hinge tests a cheaper plan as users become more fed up paying for dating apps | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Hinge is testing a lower‑priced subscription tier that adds extra filters and custom location boundaries, a move announced during Match Group’s Q3 2026 earnings call. The new plan is aimed at women and price‑sensitive users, as Match Group notes Hinge’s revenue per payer is nearly twice Tinder’s but its payer penetration is lower. Despite Hinge’s strong growth—12% YoY increase in global monthly active users, 19% rise in direct revenue, and 2.3 million paid subscribers—the company is shifting strategy to broaden its paying base amid widespread subscription fatigue. The initiative comes alongside Match Group’s broader efforts to diversify engagement with features like Group Hangouts, Events, and real‑time adaptive recommendations.
key_points: Hinge’s new tier adds filters and custom location boundaries to attract price‑sensitive users
Match Group highlights Hinge’s high revenue per payer but low payer penetration compared to Tinder

posts.title: A fresh wave of cyberattacks has hit Europe's supermarket refrigerators, destroying food across countries | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: A second wave of cyberattacks targeted supermarket refrigerators across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden, raising temperatures and causing widespread food spoilage. Supermarket giants Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt confirmed the hacks, which were carried out by changing defrost settings on Danfoss‑made units that no longer receive security updates. The incidents follow a similar French attack last month and highlight how weak IoT security can disrupt the food supply chain. The attacks underscore the real‑world impact of cyber threats on everyday infrastructure and consumer goods.
key_points: Hackers raised temperatures on Danfoss refrigerators, causing food spoilage in multiple European countries
Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt confirmed heavy losses and the manipulation of defrost settings
Earlier France and US UNFI attacks show a growing trend of IoT‑based supply‑chain disruptions
Weak cybersecurity practices in IoT devices enable real‑world damage to food and logistics

posts.title: OpenAI is finally merging ChatGPT's Chat and Work tabs | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: OpenAI is set to merge the Chat and Work tabs in the ChatGPT desktop app, a change that will let users move from idea exploration to execution in a single interface. The new experience will first be available to a select group of users for feedback before a wider rollout. Both ChatGPT and Codex will now draw tokens from the same allowance pool, which may cause some users to see more frequent reset waits. Anthropic has already merged similar functions in Claude, highlighting a trend toward unified AI workspaces.

posts.title: Ford launches a 'privacy promise' and explains how and why it uses customer data | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Ford has announced a new "privacy promise" that commits to safeguarding vehicle data and giving customers control over what they share, accompanied by a dedicated website that explains data collection, usage, and settings. The initiative comes as Ford prepares to launch a new generation of connected cars on its universal electric vehicle platform, aiming to address growing consumer concerns about data privacy and to differentiate itself from competitors. Ford’s chief privacy officer, Kristin Jones, emphasized that the company will not monetize data or share driving information with third‑party brokers, and that opting out of certain data sharing will disable features such as real‑time navigation and roadside assistance. The move follows a recent $220 million settlement by General Motors over data‑sharing practices and reflects a broader industry push toward clearer consumer communication about data use.
key_points: Ford launches a privacy promise and a new website to explain data collection and give customers control over sharing
Opting out of data sharing will disable some connected features, such as real‑time navigation and roadside assistance
Ford explicitly states it will not monetize data or share driving information with third‑party brokers
The initiative follows industry scrutiny, including GM’s recent settlement, and aims to build consumer trust amid rising privacy concerns

posts.title: Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: Ukrainian startup CODE380 has unveiled the pocket‑sized D·Vision SDR, a receiver that captures live, unencrypted video from Russian drones and displays it on a screen, giving Ukrainian forces real‑time insight into drone targets. The device weighs only about 10 ounces, making it lighter than competing models that can weigh several pounds. It can intercept the new radio channels used by Russia’s Molniya drones, which began transmitting video in June, a capability that many existing detectors miss. Analysts warn that a shift to fully digital video could render such analog receivers ineffective in the future.
key_points: CODE380’s D·Vision SDR captures live video from Russian drones
The device weighs only 10 ounces, lighter than competitors
It intercepts new Molniya drone video channels introduced in June
A future move to digital video could blind analog receivers

posts.title: Elon Musk throttles Grok Bot limits due to 'unsustainably high' costs | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: Elon Musk announced that SpaceX’s Grok Bot will have its usage limits throttled after users reported their weekly caps maxing out unexpectedly. Musk confirmed on X that the cost of serving the bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue, not a glitch. SpaceX’s AI division, which now accounts for 52% of the company’s income, posted a $431 million profit but was hit by $1.2 billion of one-time Cursor acquisition costs. The company has yet to detail how subscriber limits will change going forward.

Musk said the bot’s operating cost was unsustainably high compared to revenue
SpaceX’s AI division made $431 million profit but faced $1.2 billion one-time costs
No update yet on future limit adjustments

posts.title: Northwood Space raises $375M Series C at a $2B valuation from a16z and DFJ Growth | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Northwood Space, a space‑infrastructure startup founded in 2022, closed a $375 million Series C that values the company at $2 billion. posts.title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’ | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: OpenAI is preparing a public relations campaign after the U.S. midterm elections to shape the national conversation around artificial intelligence, according to chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane. The company’s strategy includes proposals such as AI speed limits, messaging that frames AI as empowering, pushing for U.S. leadership in global standards, and rebranding its data centers as "AI compute campuses" to mitigate public unease. Lehane emphasized that communities should hold AI firms accountable so they deliver transformative benefits, and noted that the debate over data centers has prompted major cloud providers to drop NDAs in local negotiations. The rebranding effort is part of a broader effort to influence the 2028 presidential election where AI is expected to be a key issue.
key_points: OpenAI plans a PR blitz after the midterms to shape the AI debate and influence the 2028 election
Proposals include AI speed limits, empowerment messaging, global standards, and rebranding data centers as "AI compute campuses"
Chris Lehane stresses community accountability and transformative benefits from AI projects
The rebranding aims to address the unpopularity of data centers and improve public perception

posts.title: Readwise takes on Amazon's Kindle and Goodreads with its new app for book lovers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Readwise has launched Readwise Books, an app that blends an e‑book store with detailed reading analytics, positioning itself as a cross between Amazon’s Kindle and Goodreads. The beta app lets users buy, read, and track millions of e‑books from major publishers, while offering richer metrics such as words read, pace, and immersion, and AI‑powered features like session recaps and term lookups. Readwise emphasizes an open‑technology approach, providing a public API and an MCP server to enable third‑party integrations and AI agents. The service remains free for the Books app, with advanced AI features slated for a future paid tier, and is available only to invitees or existing Readwise subscribers.
key_points: Readwise Books combines an e‑book store with in‑depth reading analytics, aiming to rival Kindle and Goodreads
The app offers AI‑driven features such as session recaps, definitions, and translations, currently available for HarperCollins titles

posts.title: Omen AI adds liquid know-how in $16 million Aquatic Labs acquisition | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Omen AI, a 2024 startup that builds real‑time water‑sensor technology for data‑center cooling, has acquired competitor Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash‑and‑stock deal, after raising $31 million in Series A funding. The merger combines Omen’s element‑detection sensors with Aquatic Labs’ alkalinity‑testing unit to deliver a richer, automated view of cooling fluids, with a product slated for market launch early next year. Omen’s first sensors will target data centers drawing 250‑300 MW of power—worth $5‑$7 billion—by year‑end, with a goal of covering 1 GW of chips by 2027, aiming to reduce costly downtime and water waste. The move positions Omen to capture a share of the projected $4 trillion AI infrastructure spend while expanding its impact beyond data centers into responsible water management.
key_points: Omen AI acquires Aquatic Labs for $16 million, merging complementary real‑time water‑sensor tech
The combined sensor will monitor both elemental composition and alkalinity, offering a fuller picture of cooling fluid health
Omen plans to deploy its first sensors in 250‑300 MW data‑center sites by year‑end, targeting 1 GW by 2027
The acquisition supports Omen’s strategy to improve uptime and reduce water‑related downtime costs in a growing AI infrastructure market

posts.title: Data centers are now a midterm issue, even in Brooklyn | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: A Brooklyn mid‑term election event highlighted how data centers and AI have become political flashpoints, with attendees debating the rapid expansion of tech infrastructure and its social impact. A recent Data Center Watch report cited nearly $200 billion in projects stalled or blocked in early 2026 due to community and political pushback, prompting states such as Pennsylvania, Georgia, Texas, New York, and Virginia to consider stricter guardrails and transparency. Panelists and city officials expressed concerns over secret deals, zoning opacity, environmental and health risks, and the perceived loss of local control, while some labor groups noted temporary job creation. The conversation underscored that AI and data centers are now election‑relevant issues that could sway voter sentiment on November 3.
key_points: Data centers and AI have become a key mid‑term election issue, influencing voter sentiment in November 2026
Nearly $200 billion in data center projects were delayed or blocked in the first half of 2026 due to political and community opposition
States including Pennsylvania, Georgia, Texas, New York, and Virginia are exploring new regulations and transparency requirements for data center development
Public backlash centers on perceived tech monopolies, environmental and health risks, and the loss of local control over community projects

posts.title: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data center pollution to move forward | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: A federal judge rejected xAI’s motion to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit that accuses the SpaceX‑owned company of operating 35 gas turbines at its Colossus data center outside Memphis without the required permits, citing statutory standing under the Clean Air Act. Judge Debra M. Brown ruled that the turbines are not considered mobile sources under Mississippi’s implementation plan and that citizen suit plaintiffs have the right to sue for environmental harm. The decision follows a similar denial of a DOJ motion to dismiss earlier this month and underscores growing public and legal pressure on data centers for pollution compliance. The ruling is seen as a win for the NAACP and a signal that environmental lawsuits against tech firms may gain traction amid rising scrutiny of data center emissions.
key_points: Judge Debra M. Brown denied xAI’s motion to dismiss, allowing the NAACP lawsuit to proceed under the Clean Air Act.
xAI’s turbines are not exempt as mobile sources, and the plaintiffs have statutory standing to sue.
The decision follows a prior DOJ dismissal denial and reflects increasing scrutiny of data center pollution.

posts.title: In one of the largest deals in tech history, Marvell buys Lumentum for $115B | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Marvell has agreed to acquire optical chip and networking equipment maker Lumentum in an all‑stock deal valued at $115 billion enterprise value, or about $80 billion equity. The transaction, one of the largest tech deals ever, will give Marvell 4.5 shares for each Lumentum share and positions the company as a leader in AI connectivity. Nvidia, a common shareholder, has already invested $2 billion in each firm to bolster their laser and optical networking capabilities. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2028, pending shareholder and regulatory approval.
key_points: Marvell acquires Lumentum for $115 billion enterprise value, $80 billion equity
Deal includes 4.5 Marvell shares per Lumentum share
Nvidia invested $2 billion in both companies
Closing expected in first half of 2028

posts.title: SpaceX reportedly wants to buy Boost Mobile to compete with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: SpaceX is reportedly looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar to add terrestrial cellular coverage to its Starlink network, a move that could push the company into fourth place among U.S. wireless providers. The acquisition would give SpaceX an instant subscriber base of about 7.5 million customers and access to the tower leases that Boost Mobile uses from AT&T and T‑Mobile, which are currently nontransferable. This follows SpaceX’s $17 billion spectrum purchase from EchoStar and its 2024 rollout of satellite access for T‑Mobile subscribers. Major carriers rejected Musk’s offers for network capacity, so the Boost deal would be the last critical piece needed for full nationwide phone coverage.
key_points: SpaceX seeks to acquire Boost Mobile to gain terrestrial network access and a 7.5 million‑user base
The deal would give SpaceX immediate tower coverage across 48 states, complementing Starlink’s satellite reach
SpaceX already bought $17 billion of spectrum from EchoStar and is expanding satellite service to T‑Mobile customers
AT&T, T‑Mobile, and Verizon rejected Musk’s capacity offers, making Boost Mobile the final piece for nationwide coverage

posts.title: 42AI comes out of stealth with $62.5M and a world model that can 'predict human behavior' | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ram Iyer
posts.summary: 42AI, an Israeli startup, has emerged from stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding and a behavioral world model that predicts individual decisions by modeling underlying psychological tendencies. The system, trained on data from over 30 million people and used by ten large brokerages, claims 98 % accuracy in predicting trading flows and an F1 score of 0.8‑0.85 for trade direction and volume. 42AI’s model relies on transformer‑based architecture and a separate language model for explanations, and it does not use personally identifiable information, though it creates behavioral profiles from linked activity. While the company sees applications beyond finance in gaming, fraud prevention, and robotics, it acknowledges ethical concerns and has put in place regulations, monitoring, and an internal ethics committee.
key_points: 42AI raised $62.5 million in seed funding and launched a behavioral world model that predicts trading decisions with high accuracy
The model uses transformer architecture and a language model for explanations, and it operates on aggregated data without personal identifiers
The startup plans to expand beyond finance into gaming, fraud prevention, and robotics while addressing ethical concerns with oversight

posts.title: Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion breach | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Binance has begun phased withdrawals after a $6.3 billion hack that froze deposits and withdrawals. The exchange says it has recovered 95 % of the stolen crypto and is still sourcing the remaining assets, which are less liquid. The FBI has identified a North Korean group, TraderTraitor, as the culprit, and Binance processed $4.6 billion in withdrawals and $1 billion in deposits, leaving a net outflow of $3.6 billion. Binance will continue to strengthen security, complete the recovery, and release a detailed incident report once the investigation finishes.

95 % of stolen assets recovered, remaining assets still being sourced
FBI links hack to North Korean group TraderTraitor

posts.title: Exclusive: Here’s what 'renoa' — the first new fiber in 25 years — feels like | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Everbloom’s new fiber, renoa, has become the first new fiber classification in 25 years after approval by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, offering a washable and affordable alternative to expensive cashmere. Made from waste protein scraps such as cashmere, wool, down, and feather lint, the material is blended with a biodegradable biopolymer and extruded to mimic natural fibers. The startup, which has been developing the fiber for three years and built its own AI material‑science model, plans to launch its first consumer product—a cashmere‑renoa blend sweater—in the second quarter of 2027. Renoa’s 80/20 blend delivers a feel close to real cashmere while resisting pilling, shrinking, and requiring minimal finishing, positioning it as a sustainable, high‑performance textile for mainstream apparel.

It is produced from waste protein scraps and is washable, affordable, and biodegradable.
Everbloom is scaling up production and expects its first consumer product to hit the market in Q2 2027.

posts.title: I took two iPhones on vacation — the Duo won me over | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Sarah Perez tested Apple’s new iPhone Duo on a five‑day vacation, initially frustrated by its small screen, unoptimized apps, and the return to Touch ID, but ultimately grew to appreciate its durability and pocket‑friendly design. The $2,000 device proved surprisingly robust, surviving multiple drops on hard surfaces without damage, and its compact, squat shape fit comfortably in both front and back pockets. While the Duo’s lack of Face ID and occasional app freezes—particularly in Google Search’s AI mode—remained notable drawbacks, Perez found that most major apps were quickly updated for the new form factor and that her Apple Watch provided a convenient alternative for authentication. The experience highlighted the psychological switching cost of moving from a high‑end iPhone 17 Pro Max to an experimental device, yet Perez concluded that the Duo’s strengths ultimately won her over.

Users may face frustrations with small screen real estate, unoptimized apps, and the return to Touch ID, especially during payments.
Major apps quickly updated for Duo, but early reviews noted black bars on non‑optimized apps and occasional freezes in Google Search’s AI mode.

posts.title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold: Sturdy rectangle in a wide, wide world | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta

The phone boasts a 48‑megapixel main sensor, 30× Super‑Res Zoom, and a three‑fold increase in durability thanks to a glass‑ceramic cover and glass‑fiber composite back. posts.title: OpenAI reportedly lowers funding target for new round | TechCrunch

posts.summary: OpenAI has cut its latest funding round target from the previously reported $30 billion to $20 billion, with the first close expected to be even lower. posts.title: From restaurant guides to payments, here’s how TikTok is building a super app | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik

posts.title: Pile-ins, payouts, and pacing pressure: the investors behind the VCs open up | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: Limited partners are currently pouring capital into a handful of AI companies, notably OpenAI and Anthropic, creating unprecedented concentration in venture portfolios. The rapid rise in valuations has prompted LPs to accelerate fund cycles, with some returning capital in as little as 12 to 18 months, a pace that raises concerns about risk and distribution timing. Despite the speed, many LPs view the consolidation as a natural evolution of the power‑law nature of venture investing, though they remain wary of potential downturns. posts.title: Nvidia weighs playing the cosigner for Nscale’s AI data center in West Virginia | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta

posts.title: Applebee's exposed customers' personal data after leaving database password in app | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: Applebee’s fixed a security flaw that allowed anyone to access its customer database after a researcher discovered a hardcoded credential in the chain’s Android app. The exposed data included names, email addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, ZIP codes, veteran status, login counts, account creation dates, and recent IP addresses. Applebee’s and parent Dine Brands said they investigated the issue and found no evidence of unauthorized access, but the exact number of affected customers remains unknown; the rewards program had 8.5 million members last year. The incident underscores the risks of hardcoding credentials and the need for proper vulnerability disclosure channels.

Applebee’s and Dine Brands investigated and found no evidence of a breach yet.

posts.title: Google's first data center satellite is online and writing poetry | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Google’s Suncatcher prototype satellite, launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 in early October, is now online and communicating with the ground while carrying four Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) that can generate up to 1 kW of power. The satellite’s first test involved asking Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4 model to compose a haiku about space, demonstrating the ability to run inference workloads in orbit, though only one TPU can be powered on for about 20 minutes at a time due to power constraints. Engineers are now evaluating how the chips perform under thermal stress and space radiation, which can cause bit flips that corrupt data, and the results will inform plans to launch two additional, higher‑power satellites in 2027 with inter‑satellite optical links. The project is part of Google’s broader vision for orbital data centers and is closely tied to SpaceX’s Starship development, with Alphabet holding a significant stake in the launch provider.

posts.title: Intel's stock crashes, knocking $12B from government's stake | TechCrunch
posts.author: Julie Bort
posts.summary: Intel’s shares plunged about 28% on Friday after the company issued a weaker‑than‑expected fourth‑quarter outlook, causing the U.S. government’s 10% stake to lose roughly $12 billion in value. The downgrade came as Intel projected revenue of $15‑$16 billion versus analysts’ $17 billion estimate and warned its gross‑margin would fall to 37% from 43%, while it expected no positive cash flow. Despite the sharp drop, the government still holds a profitable position, with Intel up more than 70% year‑to‑date, and Nvidia’s stake also saw a modest decline. The company cited a PC slowdown driven by high memory prices and AI demand, but noted a 78% jump in data‑center revenue, though capacity expansion is delayed until new fabs become operational in 2028.
key_points: Intel’s stock fell 28% after a weaker Q4 outlook, wiping $12 billion off the government’s stake.
The company warned of lower revenue ($15‑$16 billion) and a margin drop to 37%, with no expected positive cash flow.

posts.title: Anthropic expected to receive high 'junk' rating from credit agencies following IPO, FT report says | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Anthropic is expected to receive a high "junk" rating from credit agencies after its IPO, according to a Financial Times report. Blackstone, the anchor investor in a $63 billion chip‑financing deal, now predicts a double‑B range rating, a top tier of speculative junk, after previously saying the company would be investment‑grade before 2027. A high junk rating would raise borrowing costs and make it harder for Anthropic to finance its large compute‑spending spree. The filing for the IPO earlier this week has intensified speculation about the impact on the broader AI industry.

posts.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: Investors are growing uneasy about the massive AI infrastructure spend announced by Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft, which together plan over $740 billion in capital expenditures this year. The news has triggered a sharp sell‑off, with the Nasdaq falling 2.9% and major chip stocks like Nvidia, Broadcom, and Qualcomm dropping 4–11%, while Alphabet’s shares plunged 12% and wiped out $500 billion in market value. posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Ollie, a privacy‑focused AI assistant startup, announced it will shut down on November 6 after a week of announcement. Co‑founder Bill Lennon said the small team built an impressive personal assistant, but competition from larger players like Muse and Instinct made it hard to raise capital and stand out. The app offered a subscription‑based service that integrated email, calendar, appointment booking, meal planning, bill payments, and planned household budgeting, and was one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2 compliance. Users will receive instructions to export data and receive refunds.

posts.title: Satlyt takes another step toward turning satellites into space data centers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Satlyt, a 2024 startup founded by former Google and SpaceX engineer Rama Afullo, demonstrated its software’s ability to orchestrate computing tasks across multiple satellites during a NASA‑funded test that ran on a physical computer aboard a spacecraft. The experiment, conducted in partnership with the University of Houston, showed the system could generate task‑allocation plans in orbit while accounting for limited compute, intermittent communication, and user‑defined constraints. Although the software successfully executed and returned results to Earth, the team identified a timing‑reference bug and noted that further validation is needed before deploying the technology on real missions. Satlyt aims to turn spacecraft into virtual data centers that can run AI and other applications onboard, reducing reliance on downlinks and enabling faster, more efficient data delivery from space to Earth.

posts.title: Zest's new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Zest, a restaurant discovery app launched in November 2024, has unveiled an AI‑powered "restaurant concierge" that operates via text messages, allowing users to receive personalized recommendations and book tables directly through services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms. The concierge pulls data from users’ credit‑card transactions via Plaid to build a taste profile, enabling it to suggest restaurants based on cuisine, location, dietary needs, and even group preferences in group chats. The startup, backed by $1.8 million in pre‑seed funding from Alexis Ohanian’s 776 and Steve Jang’s Kindred Ventures, plans to expand beyond dining to other recommendation domains while monetizing through booking and future ordering revenue streams. posts.title: North Korean hackers blamed for stealing record $6.3B in Binance breach | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker

The prestigious firm is winding down after its heir apparent declined the leadership role, top lawyers departed, and a planned merger with Willkie Farr & Gallagher fell through.
